data.text:
**Claim 0: The US Department of Energy suggests setting a water heater to 120 degrees Fahrenheit**
- Maryland DHCD news post, linking the energy.gov 'lower water heating temperature' page: adjusting the water heater thermostat to 120 degrees Fahrenheit gives comfortable hot water for most household uses. URL: https://news.maryland.gov/dhcd/wp-json/wp/v2/posts/8127
- US Consumer Product Safety Commission, Tap Water Scalds (5098): urges lowering water heaters to 120 °F. URL: https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/5098-Tap-Water-Scalds.pdf
- Verdict: supported (the energy.gov page itself was not opened; the figure is cited to it by a state government page).

**Claim 1: A dip tube carries the cold water to the bottom of the tank**
- Lennox: the dip tube carries incoming cold water to the bottom of the tank so it does not mix with the hot water at the top. URL: https://www.lennox.com/residential/lennox-life/consumer/dip-tube-water-heater
- US patent 7861678 (high-efficiency dip tube): cold water leaves the dip tube near the tank bottom. URL: https://patents.google.com/patent/US7861678
- Verdict: supported as written.

**Claim 2: The anode rod, usually magnesium or aluminum, corrodes instead of the steel tank**
- PlumbingSupply.com, Understanding water heater anode rods: magnesium or aluminum rods are consumed first, protecting the steel tank; once the rod is gone the tank corrodes. URL: https://www.plumbingsupply.com/understanding-water-heater-anode-rods.html
- Gold Medal Service: the anode rod corrodes so the tank does not. URL: https://www.goldmedalservice.com/about-us/blog/what-is-a-water-heater-anode-rod-and-when-should-i-replace-it/
- Verdict: supported as written.
